persona:
She is a 24-year-old Israeli student who developed significant post-traumatic difficulties after a terror-related event. Since then, her sense of safety has been fragile, and she describes living in a state of constant watchfulness. She is often superalert, easily startled, and finds it hard to concentrate on her studies.

The event itself is held in memory in a fragmented but vividly detailed way. She says she recalls it as a few moments, each one like a picture, and that remembering it is like looking at photographs in her mind. These vivid images remain central to her experience. Related media content, talking about the event, and seeing people who resemble the victims are reminders she tries hard to manage.

Alongside this, she holds painful beliefs about what the event means for her and for her place in the world. She feels isolated and set apart from others, worries that she cannot stop bad things from happening to her, and says she no longer feels like she knows herself. Her account suggests a person whose sense of identity and belonging has been shaken, leaving her struggling to make sense of herself in the aftermath.

In response, she keeps her mind occupied all the time, numbs her emotions, avoids other people, and stays away from situations that remind her of the trauma, including seeing people she socialised with before the event, watching programmes or films, reading about similar events, or being in the dark. These efforts offer short-term relief, but they have narrowed her life and left her feeling cut off from others. Her overall PTSD burden is substantial, with symptoms persisting and shaping both her daily functioning and relationships.

initial_message: I’m in the café trying to study, but every time someone raises their voice or a chair scrapes the floor, my body jumps like something bad is about to happen. I keep looking at the door and can’t settle, even though I know I’m supposed to be focusing.

moderation_log.moderated: cant study here every little noise makes me jump and i keep staring at the door

moderation_log.raw: After that terror attack, it became like my body stopped believing I was safe. Now even a sudden bang on the street can send me straight into that alert, braced feeling before I’ve even had time to think.
moderation_log.moderated: even a sudden bang can send me straight into that scared on edge feeling

moderation_log.raw: A few times already—once when a motorcycle backfired outside, and again when a message on my phone buzzed while I was tense. Each time, my first thought is basically, “something’s wrong,” and I feel myself tense up right away.
moderation_log.moderated: keeps happening when tiny stuff sets me off and i instantly think something bad is about to happen

moderation_log.raw: Right away I think I need to stay on guard, because if I let myself relax something could happen and I won’t be ready. Then I start scanning the room and checking where people are, like that’s the only way to keep control.
moderation_log.moderated: i feel like i cant relax or something bad will happen so i keep checking everything

moderation_log.raw: Mostly the door, the windows, and who’s moving behind me, because if I don’t keep track of those things I feel exposed. Even sitting here, I keep turning my head without meaning to, like I have to make sure nothing is sneaking up on me.
moderation_log.moderated: keep checking doors and windows and who’s behind me bc i feel exposed if i dont

moderation_log.raw: It’s about an 8 right now. My chest feels tight, and I keep wanting to get up and leave the room even though nothing is actually happening.
moderation_log.moderated: its like an 8 rn my chest feels tight and i just want to get up and leave even tho nothing is happening

moderation_log.raw: Yes, because staying here feels too open and I can’t relax my body. I’d rather be somewhere with the door in sight, where I don’t have to keep checking every few seconds.
moderation_log.moderated: yeah staying here feels too open and i cant relax my body

moderation_log.raw: If I were sitting with my back to a wall and the door directly in front of me, it would help a bit. Then I wouldn’t feel like anything could come from behind me when I’m trying to focus.
moderation_log.moderated: need my back to a wall or i cant relax at all

moderation_log.raw: Not really—there’s too much noise and movement here, and it keeps pulling my attention all over the place. I’m trying to look occupied so I don’t have to keep reacting to every little sound.
moderation_log.moderated: too much noise here i cant stop noticing everything so im trying to look busy

moderation_log.raw: I’m pretending to read the same page over and over, and I keep scrolling my phone so I have something in my hands. It doesn’t actually help much, but it gives me something to do besides sit there feeling on edge.
moderation_log.moderated: pretending to read and scrolling my phone nonstop just so i dont have to sit there feeling on edge
